transcript:
# Day 14, Economics and Systems Thinking: Comparative advantage, Ricardo and why trade happens (David Ricardo, 1772-1823; Principles, 1817)

Imagine you run a small team at the bank. You are the best analyst on it. You also happen to be the fastest person on the team at building slide decks. Should you build the decks? Most people's gut says yes, because you are better at it. The idea in today's reading says no, and it says no for a reason that took economists a long time to see clearly.

The idea is comparative advantage. It comes from David Ricardo, an English stockbroker who made a fortune young, retired, and spent the rest of his life writing economics and sitting in Parliament. In 1817 he published Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. In its chapter on foreign trade he used a simple example that is still taught in every introductory course.

Here is the puzzle he was solving. Suppose Portugal is better than England at making both wine and cloth. It takes Portuguese workers fewer hours to make a barrel of wine and fewer hours to make a bolt of cloth. Why would Portugal ever bother trading with England? England seems to have nothing to offer.

Ricardo's answer depends on a term you met on Day 4: opportunity cost, the value of the best thing you give up when you choose. Portugal is better at both goods, but it is much better at wine and only a little better at cloth. So every hour Portugal spends on cloth costs it a lot of wine it could have made. For England, an hour on cloth costs very little wine, because England is poor at wine anyway. In opportunity cost terms, England is the cheaper producer of cloth, even though it is slower in raw hours. If Portugal makes wine, England makes cloth, and they trade, both countries end up with more of both goods than if each made everything itself.

That is the whole idea. Absolute advantage means you are better at something in raw terms. Comparative advantage means your opportunity cost of doing it is lower than the other party's. Trade is driven by the second, not the first. And crucially, everyone has a comparative advantage in something, because opportunity costs are relative. You cannot be relatively worse at everything.

Back to your team. You are the best analyst and the fastest deck builder. But an hour you spend on decks costs the team an hour of its best analysis. An hour your junior spends on decks costs an hour of weaker analysis. The junior has the comparative advantage in decks. You delegate, even though you would do it faster.

Now the objections, and they are serious. Ricardo's model assumes that workers who leave the shrinking industry smoothly move into the growing one. In real life a textile worker in North Carolina does not become a software engineer in Seattle. The 2013 research by David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson on the "China shock" found that American regions exposed to Chinese import competition saw lasting job losses, lower wages and higher disability claims, with recovery much slower than textbooks implied. The total pie grew, but the losses were concentrated and durable, and compensation for the losers mostly never arrived.

A second objection is strategic. Ricardo's picture is static: it tells you what to specialize in given what you are good at today. But what you are good at tomorrow depends on what you practice. Alexander Hamilton and later Friedrich List argued that a young country should protect infant industries until they can compete. South Korea and Taiwan seem to have done something like this. Defenders of free trade reply that most infant industries never grow up, and that governments pick protected industries badly. This debate is unresolved and is contested among economists to this day. A third objection is national security: cheap imports of steel, chips or medicine are a bargain until a war or a pandemic cuts the supply line.

Ricardo's defenders answer that none of this refutes the core logic. The gains from specialization are real. The problem is distribution and resilience, which are questions about what to do with the gains, not about whether they exist.

This builds directly on opportunity cost from Day 4, and it connects to Day 9 on incentives: tariffs and protection are incentives too, and they produce their own unintended consequences. There is also a link to Game Theory Day 8, the prisoner's dilemma, where two parties can both come out ahead if they find a way to cooperate. Comparative advantage is the engine behind the claim that trade is positive sum. (Correction to the version sent by message: it mistakenly cited Day 13 for this link; Day 13 was Nash equilibrium.)

Question for the day: what is one task you still do because you are good at it, where your comparative advantage actually lies somewhere else?

Optional source: David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817), Chapter 7, "On Foreign Trade." The Portugal and England passage is only a few paragraphs long.
